function.description: This function compares two TypeScript declaration objects to determine if they have identical declaration flags, taking into account specific allowances for differences in optionality between parameters and variable declarations. Note that the provided function is in JavaScript syntax.

left.description: The first TypeScript declaration object to compare. This parameter can be of any type of JavaScript object in string representation.

message.content:
Sure! To compare the declaration flags of a **parameter** (`parameterObject`) and a **variable declaration** (`variableDeclarationObject`), you’ll want to feed both objects (in string form) into the `areDeclarationFlagsIdentical` helper. Here’s a quick rundown of what the function checks:

| Flag | What it means | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|----------------|
| `optional` | Whether the element can be omitted (`?`). | Parameters may be optional while variables cannot. |
| `private`, `protected`, `public` | Access modifiers. | Must match exactly. |
| `async` | Whether the element is asynchronous (`async`). | Only applies to functions/methods. |
| `abstract` | Whether the element is abstract (`abstract`). | Only applies to classes/abstract methods. |
| `readonly` | Whether the element is read‑only (`readonly`). | Applies to properties and parameters. |
| `static` | Whether the element is static (`static`). | Only applies to class members. |

The function will return `true` if all relevant flags match, allowing for the special rule that a *parameter* can be optional even when the corresponding *variable* isn’t.

---

### How to use it

```ts
import { areDeclarationFlagsIdentical } from "./path/to/functions";

const parameterObject = {
    name: "foo",
    type: "string",
    optional: true,
    private: false,
    protected: false,
    public: true,
    async: false,
    abstract: false,
    readonly: false,
    static: false
};

const variableDeclarationObject = {
    name: "foo",
    type: "string",
    optional: false,   // <-- this is ignored for variables
    private: false,
    protected: false,
    public: true,
    async: false,
    abstract: false,
    readonly: false,
    static: false
};

const result = areDeclarationFlagsIdentical({
    left: JSON.stringify(parameterObject),
    right: JSON.stringify(variableDeclarationObject)
});

console.log(result); // true or false
```

> **Tip:** If you’re working directly in a TypeScript environment, you can skip the `JSON.stringify` step and pass the objects themselves; just make sure the function signature matches your setup.
